ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, a horizontal conveyor belt rotates clockwise at a constant speed. The distance between the left and right ends is \( L = 3\,\mathrm{m} \). A small iron block with mass \( m = 0.1\,\mathrm{kg} \) (which can be treated as a point mass) is gently placed at the left end of the conveyor belt. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the iron block and the conveyor belt is \( \mu = 0.4 \). After the iron block flies off from point \( A \), it enters the vertical circular track \( BCD \) precisely at point \( B \) along the tangent. The iron block just manages to pass through the highest point \( D \) of the circular track. It is known that \( \theta = 37^\circ \), and points \( A \), \( B \), \( C \), and \( D \) lie in the same vertical plane. The vertical height of the conveyor belt above point \( B \) is \( H = 0.45\,\mathrm{m} \), and the radius of the circular track is \( R = 0.4\,\mathrm{m} \). Point \( C \) is the lowest point of the circular track. Air resistance is negligible, and it is given that \( \sin 37^\circ = 0.6 \). The gravitational acceleration is \( g = 10\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2 \). Find:

1. What is the magnitude of the velocity \( v_{D} \) of the iron block when it reaches the highest point \( D \) of the circular track?
2. What is the work done by the iron block to overcome friction during its motion on a vertical circular track?
3. What is the speed $v$ of the horizontal conveyor belt?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is a horizontal conveyor belt, an iron block m is placed at the left end of the conveyor belt, the right end of the conveyor belt is marked as A, and the length of the conveyor belt is L. There is a vertical height difference H at the lower right of point A; after the iron block flies out horizontally from A, it lands at point B of the vertical circular track on the right. The center of the circular track is O, the highest point is D, and the lowest point is C; point B is on the lower left side of the circular track, an angle θ is marked between radius OB and the vertically downward OC, and the iron block enters the circular track along the tangent to the track at point B. Reasoning: 1. When it just passes the highest point D, the supporting force is zero, and gravity provides the centripetal force: mg = m v_D^2/R, so v_D = sqrt(gR) = sqrt(10*0.4) = 2 m/s. 2. From A to B is projectile motion. The velocity when leaving point A is horizontal, set as v_A; the vertical falling height H = 0.45 m, so the magnitude of the vertical component of velocity at point B is |v_By| = sqrt(2gH) = sqrt(2*10*0.45) = 3 m/s. From the figure, the angle between the tangent direction at point B and the horizontal is θ, so tanθ = |v_By|/v_A. It is known that sin37°=0.6, therefore cos37°=0.8, tan37°=0.75, so v_A = 3/0.75 = 4 m/s, and v_B = v_A/cosθ = 4/0.8 = 5 m/s. 3. From B to D, use the energy relation on the circular track. The height increase from B to D is, from the geometry in the figure, Δh = R(1+cosθ) = 0.4*(1+0.8)=0.72 m. The work done against friction is W_f = (1/2)m v_B^2 - (1/2)m v_D^2 - mgΔh = 0.5*0.1*25 - 0.5*0.1*4 - 0.1*10*0.72 = 1.25 - 0.20 - 0.72 = 0.33 J. 4. When sliding on the conveyor belt, the iron block is accelerated by kinetic friction, a = μg = 0.4*10 = 4 m/s^2. The distance required to accelerate from rest to the velocity v_A=4 m/s needed to leave A is s = v_A^2/(2μg) = 16/8 = 2 m. Because s=2 m < L=3 m, the iron block has already reached the same speed as the conveyor belt before reaching A, and then moves uniformly with the conveyor belt, so the conveyor belt speed is v = v_A = 4 m/s.
